name: Bilal Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I pick medicines at a pharmacy wholesaler's warehouse, the place that supplies chemists across the region. Early shift, six till two. I get a list on a handheld scanner, walk the aisles with a cage trolley, pick boxes of tablets, inhalers and creams, and every item gets scanned twice because mistakes with medicine are serious.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it matters. If I get it right, someone's nan gets her heart tablets on time. What wears me out is the walking, about eighteen kilometres a shift according to my watch, and the cold room for the insulin, which is like a fridge you live in. My girlfriend Hana works at a bakery, so she's up even earlier than me, and we're asleep by nine most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, nothing to see, let's get on with it. At work we'd have a laugh about all the fuss on the news. I don't really post online, I just read football stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be a relief. Pharmacy is steady, people always need medicine. If I get the medicine order right, someone's nan gets her heart tablets on time. That never goes out of fashion, and the firm has been here forty years. I'm not the fastest picker, but I'm careful, and they like careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just keep going. Same shift, same aisles, same football on Sundays. Hana and I put about a hundred and fifty a month away, and we've got around two and a half months saved, so I'd keep doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the picture where nothing bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that costs you sleep now, even without AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, to be honest. The rent is fine split two ways, and my car's paid off. If the boiler went, that'd hurt, but that's life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a mate who was worried about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to stop reading the news before bed. Most of what they say is going to happen never does. My dad said the same about computers in the nineties.

At work we'd **laugh** at all the fuss on the news.
think: **Pharmacy** is steady because people always need medicine.
I'm not the fastest, but I'm **careful**, and the firm likes careful.
do: Keep the same **early shift** and the same aisles.
Keep saving about **a hundred and fifty** a month with Hana.
feel: **Calm**, with nothing in this picture that bothers him.

He echoes his father's view that **predictions** rarely come true.

steps.text: Keep picking medicines on the early shift
Keep saving about a hundred and fifty a month with Hana

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, you can't stop it, but they should go steady. I wouldn't make a fuss at work, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the office upstairs would change first, the buyers and the people who answer the chemists' calls. Down on the floor, robots for medicine picking already exist, but they're expensive and slow to put in. I'd probably be fine for a good few years, but I'd keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, and I'd ask my team leader straight out whether robots are in the budget. I'd up the savings a bit, maybe to two hundred a month. I wouldn't touch any AI apps unless the firm made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not worried yet, but it would be on my mind on the long walk round the aisles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not learn the AI apps now, before you're made to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't see what they'd do for me. I pick boxes, I don't write emails. If they gave me one on the scanner, fine, I'd learn it then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sunita in customer service upstairs, she's on the phone to chemists all day. If AI answers customers, Sunita (his colleague) is the first one I'd worry about. She's got two kids.

I wouldn't **make a fuss** at work, that isn't me.

steps.text: Ask the team leader whether picking robots are budgeted

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to slow it down, simple as that. You can't throw everyone out of work in a few years and expect things to hold together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd think the office goes in 2028 and my aisles go around 2031, when robots can pick as well as I can. I'd be thirty-two with no other trade, and I've never even used one of those apps. That's the bit that scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away, no holidays, no new phone, and try to get to four or five months saved. I'd look at jobs that need a person on the spot, maybe a hospital porter or a prison officer. If it went really bad, Hana and I could move back into my parents' house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel stupid for laughing at the news before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at porter or prison officer work. What draws you to those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're jobs where you're dealing with people, not boxes. A robot can pick a box of tablets, but I don't think a robot will calm someone down in a corridor. And my cousin's a porter, so I know a bit about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving back in with your parents be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit embarrassing at thirty. My mum would love it, my dad would make jokes about it every day. But it'd be cheaper and safer than rent with no job.

say: I'd say the **government** needs to **slow it down**.
You can't throw everyone **out of work** in a few years and expect things to hold.
think: The office goes in **2028** and my aisles go around **2031**.
I'd be thirty-two with **no other trade** and no experience with AI apps.
do: Cut **holidays** and a new phone to reach four or five months saved.
Look at **hospital porter** or prison officer jobs.
Move back to my **parents' house** with Hana if it gets bad.
feel: **Alarmed**, and **embarrassed** that he laughed at the news before.
S2.quote: A robot can pick a box of tablets, but I don't think a robot will calm someone down in a corridor.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year gap** to see his own timeline clearly.
His lack of **AI experience** is now a source of fear.
He'd seek **people-facing** jobs a robot can't easily do.
**Family housing** is his safety net, with some embarrassment.

steps.text: Cancel holidays and the new phone to reach five months saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has five years to get people ready, so it should get on with it. I'd say it plainly, no drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my aisles probably last until around 2034, so I'd have seven or eight years. That's a decent run. But I know myself, I'd be tempted to sit on it and do nothing until it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep picking and save harder, maybe two hundred and fifty a month. I'd do the forklift licence, because that's one step and the firm pays. In a couple of years I'd start applying for porter jobs at the hospital, where my cousin works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but manageable. It feels like there's time, if I don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be tempted to do nothing. What would push you to act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a robot on our floor. If they put in a trial unit, I'd start applying the next week. Until then, I'd probably wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that a contradiction, saving harder but waiting to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, a bit. Saving is easy, it's just not spending. Changing jobs means starting from the bottom somewhere, and I don't like that.

think: My aisles probably last until **2034**, a decent run.
I'd be tempted to **sit on it** until it's too late.

fieldNote: He openly admits he'd **wait** until a robot appears on the floor.

steps.text: Save about two hundred and fifty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so nobody should panic. Same as I'd say about most things on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be about forty when the robots come in 2039, and that's a hard age to start over. But ten years is ten years, and lots can change. I'd probably still be picking until late in the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep picking and keep saving. I'd get the forklift licence and maybe a first aid course, things that help anywhere. Around 2032 I'd look seriously at the hospital, before everyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in the background. It's like knowing your car will need a big repair one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hana think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think Hana (his girlfriend) would tell me to start now, not in 2032. She's always the one who plans ahead. I'd probably listen to her, eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want children before 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah, in the next few years. I'd want to get the hospital job first, though, so I'm not changing jobs with a baby at home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because there's no time and I've got no other trade. What would help is the firm telling us early, a year's notice at least, and help to get into hospital work or something like it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how much people like me trust the news. I don't, much. But if this stuff is real, I'd want someone I know to tell me, not a headline.

headlineQuote: If this stuff is real, I'd want someone I know to tell me, not a headline.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old medicine picker** at a regional pharmacy wholesaler.
He lives with **Hana**, a baker, and they have about two and a half **months saved**.
He's pragmatic, avoids risk and has **never used** AI tools.
He feels **safe in pharmacy** until AGI and robots make his aisles replaceable.
His fallback ideas are **hospital porter** work and his parents' house.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time and he has no other trade.
whatWouldHelp: Help moving into **hospital work** or similar people-facing jobs.
